title: An AI-native org isn't everyone using AI — it's assuming the org doesn't exist and rebuilding it
dek: Locke merged HR and IT into HARO, put a technical founder-type in charge of people and AI; circle leads get the bonus pool to allocate, and hiring requires proving AI can't do the job.
why: A 12-year hardware company's founder on the concrete mechanics of rewriting an org: HARO, circles, AI management trainees, how FDEs actually land — with details and the pitfalls.
who: Founders, HR leaders and business owners pushing an AI org transformation, especially at hardware or consumer electronics companies that want to move on org design but don't know where to start.
skip: After 1:04:25 the chit-chat and outro music can be skipped.

points.h: AI-native starts by assuming the org doesn't exist
points.body: Chen Bin's definition of an AI-native organization is not ‘everyone should use AI well’ but starting from AI and asking again: can AI do this thing, and as far as possible don't have a person do it. The harsher step is to assume the original organization and processes don't exist — ‘they shouldn't even exist’ — and go back to the state of a one-person startup to redesign roles and processes. So this is not accelerating existing processes; it's tearing the processes down first and rebuilding. He concedes this is mainly aimed at the core org builders, not a slogan shouted at everyone.

points.h: HARO's head comes from tech, not HR
points.body: Locke merged HR and IT into HARO (Human AI Resource Office), but Chen Bin stresses it is not ordinary HR+IT: the head must understand the business, and the pick was an old partner who started the company with him and has done technology, product, CEO, R&D, brand and IT. The logic is inverted — the old HR head leaned toward people and was insensitive to AI, so now a technology-oriented person runs it, with HR BPs who are sensitive to people assigned to him. Under this department sit the AIO (the former IT team, which will do Agent Builder work) on a solid line, and FDEs reporting on a dotted line.

points.h: Agent Builder and FDE are two different people in the short term
points.body: Chen Bin draws the line clearly: an Agent Builder leans technical and can build an Agent; an FDE has to go into the business front line and map out supply, planning and procurement processes, and is ideally a business expert. Long term one person might cover it; short term it must be two kinds of people working together. They did not copy Anker's approach of pulling people out of work and locking them away for a month, because they don't have that much slack; instead people from the business spend 30% to 50% of their energy doing AI-ification alongside their business work. The company also set up AI proficiency levels L1 to L4, with L2 and above called ‘AI 起航员’ (AI navigators) and above that ‘领航员’ (pilots).

points.h: Circles erase functional power; circle leads get the bonus pool
points.body: Locke's circles differ from project teams and from Huawei's matrix: a matrix is product line plus function on two axes, while a circle is a small team around an end-to-end value loop, deliberately erasing functional power and boundaries so the circle lead's power grows. The company gives a circle a bonus pool, and the circle lead decides how to split it — even how much to give himself — with HR and functional departments holding only an advisory voice. Chen Bin says at this stage the ‘fighting’ line dominates; the functional line may in future become something like a technology committee, but within six months to a year of the transformation the front line decides first.

Chen Bin says AI management trainees have used AI since they started university in 2023, have no fear of doing things, and use it more than the veterans. His words: ‘sometimes experience instead becomes a burden’, and the most troublesome are the half-baked — whose experience isn't there yet but who feel very experienced and can't change. Veterans have framework thinking and systematic thinking as a foundation, but the clear-eyed ones judge more easily which processes and which roles can be removed. The bar for AI management trainees is internal AI level L2 or above, requiring skills and the ability to build Agents; only L3 can author workflows.

points.h: R&D turns fast, marketing turns slow
points.body: Chen Bin admits transformation speed varies a lot by department: technical R&D tied to software and coding is easiest, because writing code every day gives positive feedback; marketing and brand are slow, because after publishing more content they ask ‘so what’ — did it bring revenue growth and higher bonuses. He also mentions a real conflict: people doing design and content feel AI can only accelerate volume, not raise quality, and that 60-point output doesn't stick around. His response is to give everyone an operating mindset: whether content drives conversion is the standard.

points.h: Three rounds of applications: stand up again, then sit down again
points.body: Locke ran three internal rounds of applications: the first for incremental roles, such as a dozen or two company-level Agents and the corresponding Agent Builders and FDEs; the second for roles missing after circles formed, such as an Agent Builder for content marketing; the third to keep filling gaps. Applicants first do a self-assessment to find what they're good at, then give a three-to-five-minute defense, and after the judges score, AI is used to analyze the meeting notes and the talks for matching. Of a hundred applicants, twenty or thirty may be chosen. Chen Bin says both the mechanism and the results were very good.

points.h: To hire, you must first prove AI can't do it
points.body: After a circle picks off people from an original department, if the boss wants to backfill, logically there are only two channels: take an AI management trainee, or use more AI tokens. If you really must hire again, it goes to Chen Bin for special approval, and you have to explain clearly why a management trainee won't work and why AI won't work. Chen Bin says ‘logically he has no channel left’. They plan to hire 50 AI management trainees by year-end and are already close to 20. Xiaofei's role at Locke is like a strategic HR or CHO as a service, doing the AI-native transformation together with Chen Bin.

Chen Bin says inside the company he is in fact the most radical one, and people often pull him back to be more cautious. On deposits like Huawei's IPD, his judgment is: AI can only rework processes that were already unreasonable and especially redundant; IPD itself is very reasonable and can only be accelerated. For example, SP to BP, from strategy to execution, used to take three months to half a year, now two months — a doubling of efficiency — but the nodes like 五看三定 are still there, just three weeks becoming three days. Training a product line manager used to take 10 to 15 years, now three to five, but the rotations that must happen can't be skipped.

points.h: Not every company should run this fast
points.body: Chen Bin's advice to three kinds of bosses — milk tea shops, PCB factories, call centers — is to look at the real value AI brings in that industry: the more traditional the industry, the lower the value, and you can wait until platforms like Doubao and Volcano Engine mature and then choose, with lower trial-and-error cost. But the more frontier the tech company, the earlier it should embrace AI, because technology changes a lot and the market changes fast, and decision quality matters more. He specifically notes that before physical AI takes off, PCB factories and the like should be cautious and not move first; milk tea shops are channel- and operations-driven, and AI can quickly build a feedback loop from the user side to the supply chain side, so it matters more there.

quotes.text: I think an AI-native organization probably starts from AI first — whatever AI can do, try not to have a person do it. Think with that AI-native mindset first, and even the process, logically, should be rebuilt.

It used to be functional, right? Now I'm an end-to-end small team around a value loop, and I even deliberately erase the functional power, or the boundaries — make functional power smaller and the circle's power, or the circle lead's power, bigger.

Actually sometimes experience instead becomes a burden. It's better to have it, but the half-baked ones are the scary ones — their experience isn't there yet, but they feel they're already very experienced, right? Can't change.

As far as possible we fill it with AI, right? Prioritize using AI — whatever AI can fill, let AI fill it. Unless it can't be filled. And if it can't be filled, internally we say: either you say you'll bring in an AI management trainee to fill it, or you use more AI tokens.

It used to take at least three months to half a year; now we do SP to BP in two months, right? At least a doubling of efficiency. But the process itself hasn't changed — it's just that where I used to hold five meetings, now it's three meetings, two meetings.

Actually, look at the real value AI brings in that industry. I think the more traditional the industry, the lower the value it brings, indeed a bit lower. And if it's lower, then you can — how to put it — you can wait until these, like us, the ones who fall in the pit and play around, right? Or like Doubao, Volcano Engine, the ones doing better — then you just choose after that.
